title: What would go in the runbook for this service?
summary: Tests whether you can name concrete, actionable runbook content tied to this system's actual failure modes, not a generic "we'd document things" answer.

slides.markdown:
A runbook is judged by one test: could a 2am on-call engineer who's never touched this service follow it and actually fix the problem? "We'd document things" fails that test instantly — it names nothing concrete.

This question follows naturally once you've named a system's failure modes elsewhere in the interview: now write down what a responder actually does when one of them fires. The strong answer names real symptoms tied to this specific system, not a generic template that would apply to any service equally, which is really a signal it applies to none of them well.

Ask who the audience is: the team that owns this service, who already know its quirks, or a generalist on-call rotation covering many services who's seeing it for the first time at 2am? A runbook for a generalist needs far more context spelled out — you can't assume they know which dashboard to open first.

Ask what this service's most common historical failure modes actually are. A runbook written from imagination covers the failures you can think of; a runbook grounded in real incident history covers the failures that actually recur — which is the only test that matters for whether it'll get used.

Structure every entry the same way: **symptom** (the alert or complaint that fires), **how to confirm it** (which dashboard, which query, which log line proves this is actually what's happening), **the specific mitigation steps** (in order, most-likely-cause first), and **who or what to escalate to** if the mitigation doesn't resolve it within a stated time.

That last piece matters as much as the fix itself — a runbook that ends at "try restarting the pods" with no next step leaves a stuck engineer exactly where an undocumented incident would.

A runbook entry for "checkout p99 latency alert fires": first, check the database connection-pool dashboard — this is the most common cause historically. If it's saturated, restart the pods that are leaking connections (named specifically, not "the affected service"). If that doesn't resolve it within 10 minutes, escalate to the database on-call, with the exact channel or page to use.

Every step in that entry is something a stressed engineer can execute mechanically, in order, without having to first understand the whole system's architecture from scratch.

Without a runbook, a new on-call engineer facing a payment-gateway-timeout alert spends 25 minutes rediscovering something the team already knows tribally: this specific alert almost always means the gateway's sandbox environment leaked into the prod config.

A runbook entry — "payment-gateway timeout: check whether `GATEWAY_ENV` is set to `sandbox` in prod config; if so, flip it and redeploy" — turns that 25-minute rediscovery into a 2-minute fix. The value of a runbook is almost entirely in capturing exactly this kind of tribal knowledge before it lives only in one engineer's head.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: what belongs in a runbook versus what doesn't
slides.markdown:
| Belongs | Doesn't belong |
|---|---|
| Concrete, repeatable diagnostic steps ("check dashboard X") | Open-ended "investigate the root cause" |
| A specific mitigation ("restart pod Y", "flip flag Z") | General architecture explanations |
| A named escalation path with a time threshold | Speculative fixes nobody's confirmed work |

A runbook exists to restore service fast, not to do the follow-up root-cause work — that's the postmortem's job. If an entry reads like "look into why this happened," it isn't a runbook step, it's a reminder that this failure mode needs a real entry written after the incident.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
A runbook that's too detailed goes stale the moment the architecture changes, and once an on-call engineer catches it lying once, nobody trusts it again. A runbook that's too sparse doesn't actually help at 2am — it's a title with no steps.

| Too detailed | Too sparse |
|---|---|
| Goes stale fast as architecture evolves | Never goes stale, because it says nothing actionable |
| Erodes trust once it's caught being wrong | Erodes trust by being useless when needed |

The fix for both: keep it to the handful of failure modes that actually recur, and review it after every incident that wasn't already covered — that keeps it both current and useful.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: keeping a runbook from going stale
slides.markdown:
Tie runbook updates to the incident postmortem process itself — every new failure mode discovered during an incident gets a runbook entry written as part of closing that incident out, not as a separate, easily-forgotten chore on someone's backlog.

This works because the moment right after an incident is exactly when the details are freshest and someone has the most motivation to write them down. Making it a required postmortem field ("runbook updated: yes/no, link") rather than an optional nice-to-have is what actually makes this happen in practice rather than staying an aspiration.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: every step was followed and it still didn't fix it
slides.markdown:
This is exactly why the escalation path is part of the runbook, not an afterthought. A good entry bakes in a clear "stop and page someone with more context" threshold — a specific time limit and a specific person or channel — rather than letting the on-call engineer thrash indefinitely trying variations of the documented mitigation.

The threshold should be time-boxed and explicit: "if latency hasn't recovered within 10 minutes of the restart, page the database on-call" — not a vague "escalate if needed," which under 2am pressure often means nobody escalates until the situation is much worse.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: writing it once at launch and never touching it again
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We wrote a thorough runbook at launch — that's done."

**Why it's wrong:** the architecture keeps moving after launch — new dependencies get added, old mitigations stop applying, dashboards get renamed. A runbook frozen at launch doesn't just become useless, it becomes actively misleading: an on-call engineer following stale steps confidently might restart the wrong service or check a dashboard that no longer reflects the real bottleneck.

**Correct model:** treat the runbook as a living document, updated as part of every postmortem that surfaces something it didn't cover — a runbook is only as trustworthy as its last real-incident review.

Structure every runbook entry as symptom, how to confirm it, the specific mitigation steps, and a time-boxed escalation path — grounded in this system's real historical failures, not a generic template. Keep it to the failure modes that actually recur, and tie updates to the postmortem process so it never goes stale silently.

A runbook is for restoring service fast — open-ended "investigate the root cause" belongs in the postmortem afterward. The detection work that tells you *when* to reach for a runbook entry is covered in [how you know this system is broken](iv-detecting-its-broken).
